newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Albright to urge ASEAN to aid N.Korea nuclear pact.
newsitem.headline: Albright to urge ASEAN to aid N.Korea nuclear pact.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Friday that she would press Asian countries to contribute more to a $4.5-billion deal that has halted North Korea's nuclear programme for nearly three years.

En route to Kuala Lumpur for a meeting with Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers she told reporters she would make a new pitch for "increased participation by other countries in KEDO," the Korean Energy Development Organisation.
Her predecessor, Warren Christopher, made a similar request at last year's ASEAN meeting, but officials said this year's appeal would be more aggressive and more direct.

It would come little more than a week before the Stalinist North was due to attend a meeting in New York on August 5 to prepare for peace talks aimed at replacing the fraying armistice from the 1950-53 Korean War with a permanent peace treaty.
The United States, South Korea and China were also expected to attend.

Japan and South Korea have pledged billions of dollars, and the United States millions of dollars, towards the 1994 agreement, under which Washington vowed to provide $4.5 billion in new nuclear power plants and alternative energy supplies in return for North Korea freezing its nuclear programme.
At the time of the deal, the United States believed Pyongyang had enough capability and fuel to make one or two atomic bombs.
But other countries have dragged their feet on donations, including Asian countries whose security is directly affected by tension on the Korean peninsula.

During private sessions at ASEAN, Albright "will make specific recommendations about dollar amounts that they (ASEAN countries) could contribute", including requests for five-year commitments, one senior official said.
"ASEAN needs to play an increasingly large role in the world and in the region," he said.

He praised Indonesia for contributing, but said "other countries have not. We're calling on them to make this a major priority. Without these contributions, KEDO can't afford the heavy fuel to supplement the nuclear facilities. It's a very important issue."

The plan is to set a target for ASEAN and let the countries decide themselves how to apportion the burden, U.S. officials said. They said the need is for "tens of millions of dollars more" than has been pledged so far.

Although the United States negotiated the landmark deal with Pyongyang and is the moving force behind KEDO, Congress has been reluctant to appropriate money to meet President Bill Clinton's commitment to provide roughly $20 million to $25 million annually for the heavy fuel that is designed to meet North Korea's needs until two new nuclear power plants are on line.
ASEAN consists of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam plus Burma and Laos, which were admitted this week.
